Rubicon report

Feelings in interview I40

Question In interview I40 (man, 23, Tower Hamlets), where does the interviewee express or report their own positive, negative or mixed feelings?

For each example: its valence, a short label for the emotion, what it is about, and whether he ties it in that passage to loneliness, to feeling connected, or to neither; and how many examples of each valence, and of each link, he gives. Feelings the interviewer suggests and the interviewee does not take up, feelings attributed to other people, and purely hypothetical feelings do not count.

The interviewee in I40 gives slightly more unpleasant feelings than pleasant ones: negative (and 1 more only weakly), positive (and 1 more only weakly) and mixed. The unpleasant ones are about being among strangers or alone somewhere unfamiliar, and about crowding; the pleasant ones are about his local hang-out, time on his own, living in the area and, weakly, having a friend with him when lost. He ties to loneliness, to feeling connected (and 1 more only weakly), and to neither (and 1 more only weakly).

48 interviews in 2 groups · 12 passages coded · 8 October 2026

  • Verification in this report:
  • 10 numbers, every one counted by code. Click any number to see who it counts.
  • 12 quotations, every one found word for word in its interview. Click a numbered marker to read it in place.
  • 18 findings and 4 high-level findings, every one checked against the interviews after a second coder coded them blind.

Loneliness among strangers

His loneliness is not about having no friends but about being where he knows no one. On the tube he says "I guess I feel lonely that's the most lonely place I can kind of think of" (), and of Liverpool Street, "It just feels lonely ‘cause there’s no one I know there, not at all" (). There, he says, "I wanna quickly get in and out of that place" (I40), which he puts with the same loneliness: "seems like everyone is alone as well. That’s why I feel lonely I guess over there" (I40).

Being alone somewhere unfamiliar also makes him nervous. Split up from his friends on holiday and taking a cab on his own, "I was alone by myself so made me feel quite nervous" (). He sets this against the same situation with a friend, when "I almost didn't care" (); that passage implies ease rather than naming it, and he names it later only in a general second person: "it just makes you feel at ease" (I40).

One of the feelings he ties to being alone is pleasant. He does not mind, and sometimes wants, time by himself in familiar places: "being alone I wouldn’t say is something I don't like…sometime I’d like to… I would like to you know just go somewhere by myself" ().

Crowds and the city

Several unpleasant feelings concern crowding, and these passages do not tie them to loneliness: dislike and awkwardness when the train is packed (), stress that gives way to relief "when the space opens up" (), and dislike of the rush at Liverpool Street, "I don't really like it" (). He describes tube journeys as "something you just want to get through" (), in a general second person. Against this he says "I enjoy living here" ().

Feeling connected

Both firm feelings he ties to connection concern the local hang-out by the football pitch, where "Almost every faces are familiar face" (I40): he says he feels "most socially connected" there () and "Just very, very comfortable" (). The weak one is the ease of being lost on holiday with a friend ().

Limits

Much of what he says about fear and nervousness is in a general second person about imagined situations, which the definitions leave out; counting those would add negative feelings tied to loneliness.

How this was made

The analysis was written down as a workflow before it was counted: what to look for, how to code it, what to count. Code then counted it from the coded passages, so anyone can check a number, and another coder can follow the same definitions and code the interviews afresh.

What was read

All 48 documents, read in full: 24 male, 24 female.

Sample: One

Coding: Emotions

one row for each passage that fits; 12 rows.

The instruction a second coder would follow
Read the interview. Find every passage in which the interviewee (not the interviewer) expresses or reports a feeling of their own: a feeling they have now or have had, in their own words. Loneliness counts as a feeling. A generalised 'you' or 'it can feel' counts only where the interviewee ties it in that passage to their own experience. Do not code: feelings the interviewee imagines for a figure in a drawing or for people in general; purely hypothetical feelings ('I would feel'); feelings the interviewer puts forward that the interviewee only agrees to with 'yeah' or 'uhum'. Where the same feeling about the same thing is repeated or elaborated in follow-up answers, code it once, quoting the clearest words. Where one answer names feelings about two different things, code each. Where one answer names several feelings about the same thing, code them as one passage and name them all in the emotion label; where a later answer names a different feeling about the same thing, code that too. Code a feeling the interviewee has about another person's situation (for example, sadness at a friend's distress) as their own feeling, but not a feeling they say the other person has. A reported absence of feeling ('it doesn't make me feel anything') is not coded. For each passage, copy the words exactly and fill the columns.

Valence

Whether the feeling expressed is pleasant, unpleasant or both.

Weak: The feeling is not named as the interviewee's own but carried by a generalised 'you' about his own situation, or only implied (such as 'I almost didn't care') rather than said.

CodeMeansCountsDoes not count
PositiveA pleasant feeling: happiness, enjoyment, relief, gratitude, love, hope, ease, respect, calm acceptance.Statements such as 'I feel good, happy', 'I enjoy', 'it's alright now'.Neutral description of an activity with no feeling named or plainly expressed.
NegativeAn unpleasant feeling: sadness, loneliness, frustration, resentment, boredom, unease, longing, resignation, distress.Statements such as 'it makes me sad', 'I feel quite lonely', 'I don't feel okay'.A passage that pairs an unpleasant feeling with a pleasant or accepting one about the same thing: code mixed.
MixedPleasant and unpleasant feelings, or acceptance and hurt, expressed together about the same thing.Statements such as 'conflicting emotions' or 'I'm used to it now but sometimes it can get to me'. Also an unpleasant feeling in the past and a pleasant or accepting one now about the same thing, in the same passage ('when I was a lot younger, it did affect me ... I’m content and I feel happier').Two feelings about different things in the same answer: code each separately.

Emotion

A short label, one to three words, for the feeling, such as loneliness, frustration, gratitude, relief; where one passage names several feelings, list each.

Subject

In a few words, what the feeling is about or what brings it on, as the interviewee describes it.

Link

Whether the interviewee, in the coded passage itself, ties the feeling to loneliness or to feeling connected.

CodeMeansCountsDoes not count
LonelinessThe feeling is loneliness, or the interviewee ties it in the passage to loneliness, being alone, having no one, not fitting in, or being an outsider or 'black sheep'.'that sometimes makes me feel lonely'; 'why do I feel like an outsider'; 'I don't mind if I don't sit with anyone' (a feeling about being alone, whatever its valence). A feeling about being or working alone counts whatever its valence, including relief or enjoyment at working alone rather than with others ('much less anxious than I was when I work within a team').A feeling about a situation the interviewee elsewhere calls lonely, where this passage does not make the tie; loneliness the interviewee attributes to other people. Enjoyment of freedom or independence where the passage does not speak of being alone or without other people (code neither).
ConnectionThe interviewee ties the feeling in the passage to feeling connected, belonging, being accepted or understood, or closeness and enjoyment with other people.'a sense of belongingness'; 'I felt like they understood me'; 'I love them and trust them with everything'.Enjoyment of a place, activity or freedom with no other people named as the source of the feeling.
NeitherThe passage ties the feeling to neither loneliness nor connection.Anger at a service, guilt about family contact, anxiety about a routine, where the passage names no tie.Any passage that fits loneliness or connection.

The check

A fresh reader ruled on every place the two codings differed, and checked every sentence and quotation of the answer against the documents, correcting the coding and the answer where they were wrong. The answer above is the corrected one, recounted after the check.

For the rows: 1. For the second coder: 1. Unsettled: 0.

Rulings on the coding

  • I40, emotions.3f6c2, "the exact same situation happened to me in another holiday with my mate I was having one person with me, and I was complete I almost didn't care" (first coder: positive, ease, connection, weak; second coder: not coded). Ruled for the rows. It is his own experience, not a hypothetical, answering about his own holiday. "I almost didn't care" is the very example the valence definition gives of an implied feeling that makes a row weak. His later naming of it, "it just makes you feel at ease", is in a generalised "you", so the row stays weak. Link connection: the ease comes from having "my mate" with him, someone he could trust.
  • I40, emotions.zpkxy, "It makes me feel like…I wanna quickly get in and out of that place … That’s why I feel lonely I guess over there." (first coder: negative, "urge to get away", loneliness; second coder: not a separate row). Ruled for the second coder; row removed. This is a follow-up answer about Liverpool Street, and the feeling it names is loneliness, already coded at emotions.sm4nk ("It just feels lonely ‘cause there’s no one I know there"). The prompt says to code the same feeling about the same thing once. "Wanting to get in and out" is a wish to leave, not a further feeling. The report still quotes these words directly, as the reason he gives for the loneliness.
  • recode/unclear.md, Box 3 "scared" and the later "anxious" answers (lines 183–247, 295–299): these are in a generalised "you" or hypothetical ("if I went…"), and the only own experience he ties them to is the cab episode, already coded at emotions.cs43f. Not coded; the first coder agrees.
  • recode/unclear.md, tube "uncomfortable" (lines 165–175): this takes up the interviewer's word for the same discomfort with strangers' closeness on a crowded train as "you just feel really awkward" (emotions.bhncs). It is a repeat, so it is not coded again. "stressful … relieved" (emotions.7fyn6) names different feelings about the same thing in a later answer, which the prompt says to code. Both coders agree; the rows stand.
  • recode/unclear.md, "something you just want to get through" (emotions.bhh4s): weak is right, because the resignation is carried by a generalised "you" and only implied. Link neither is right, because the passage does not mention being alone. Stands.

Omissions found

I searched the whole interview for each count and for each "all", "both" or "only" claim. I found no passage, firm or weak, that both coders missed. These were checked and left out:

  • "You’ll be comfortable with your friends…" (line 111): a generalised "you" about a newcomer to any group, not tied to his own case in the passage.
  • "Sounds like you like seeing familiar people." / "Yeah yeah." (lines 141–143): the interviewer's suggestion, which he only agrees to.
  • "It’s not something I like." (line 151) and "lively not in a good way" (line 389): repeats of the crowding and Liverpool Street dislike rows.
  • "That's how I was feeling." (line 267): a repeat of the cab nervousness.
  • "probably the safest space it could be" (line 341): inside the same answer as "Just very, very comfortable" about the same place, so it is part of emotions.2ua92 and not a new row.
  • "I don't know if I'd be able to live in somewhere like completely isolated" (line 385): hypothetical.
  • "awkward" (line 47): a feeling given to the figure in his drawing.

Changes to answer.md

  • Opening: "mostly reports unpleasant feelings" became "slightly more unpleasant feelings than pleasant ones". With the corrected rows, negative is 5 (+1 weak) against positive 4 (+1 weak) and mixed 1, which is not "mostly".
  • Opening: "they gather around one thing: being among strangers" was overstated, since the report's own crowding section names feelings that are not about strangers. It now lists the subjects: strangers and unfamiliar places, crowding, and for the pleasant ones the hang-out, time alone, living in the area and, weakly, having a friend with him.
  • Opening counts: these recounted from the rows (negative 6→5, loneliness 5→4) after emotions.zpkxy was removed. The link sentence was reworded only.
  • "There the loneliness comes with an urge to leave … [emotions.zpkxy]": the row was removed. The sentence now quotes I40 directly, and says that he puts the wish to leave with the same loneliness ("That’s why I feel lonely I guess over there").
  • "Lost on holiday and taking a cab alone" became "Split up from his friends on holiday and taking a cab on his own", which is what he describes (line 263).
  • The "implies ease" sentence was kept, with an addition: he names the ease later only in a generalised "you" ("it just makes you feel at ease", line 287).
  • "Not every feeling about being alone is unpleasant" became "One of the feelings he ties to being alone is pleasant", so that the reader sees one of the loneliness-linked rows is positive.
  • "He likes time by himself on familiar ground" became "He does not mind, and sometimes wants, time by himself in familiar places". His words are "I wouldn’t say is something I don't like…sometime I’d like to", which is weaker than "likes".
  • "concern crowding rather than loneliness" became "these passages do not tie them to loneliness". At line 175 he does connect the discomfort to "people you don't know", so the original wording was too strong. "the city's rush" became "the rush at Liverpool Street", which is the passage's subject.
  • "He describes enduring tube journeys" became "He describes tube journeys"; "enduring" read more into the passage than it says.
  • "His positive feelings tied to connection all concern the local hang-out" was false once the weak row emotions.3f6c2 (ease with a friend on holiday) is counted. It became "Both firm feelings…", and a sentence was added naming the weak one. "where he knows almost everyone" is now his own words, "Almost every faces are familiar face".
  • Limits: cut "This is one interview, so the counts describe what one person said…", since that restates the question. The rest was reworded slightly; its substance is unchanged.

recount.py reports no faults: 10 counts written by id, and no citations, quotations or numbers out of place.

The record

Code drew this report from the run's zip, in-interview-i40-man-23-tower-hamlets-where-does-2026-10-08-d0ee0727.zip, with Rubicon 0.1.0+bfb9b34fd622. The zip's fingerprint is d0ee0727ae73bd50d92f8d9af1671ff83a0fb800f18c38e892f9e640d624ee70. It is the SHA-256 of the zip's SHA256SUMS file, which lists the SHA-256 of every other file in the zip, so changing any file breaks the match. To check that the zip is the one this report was drawn from, unzip it, run sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS, then sha256sum SHA256SUMS, and compare the result with the fingerprint above. Rubicon's own code, which is public, checks the rest: python verify.py <report> <zip> recounts every number from the coded passages in the zip, draws the report again from the zip and says whether it matches this one exactly.

What next

For the evaluator: Treat this report as a draft. Before it is final, make sense of it with the people it concerns, such as programme staff and participants: whether the findings ring true, what they leave out, and what to do about them. You can then use the Rubicon plugin to work their responses back into a revised answer.

For evaluation commissioners: Parallel to this report is a zip file (in-interview-i40-man-23-tower-hamlets-where-does-2026-10-08-d0ee0727.zip), saved in the same folder, which contains the whole run: the documents, the coded passages and the workflow that recounts every number. Its fingerprint, under How this was made, ties it to this report: change a file in either and they no longer match. With it, anyone can check every number against the coded passages, and code the documents again to the same definitions without Rubicon or any other particular software. A fresh coding will not reproduce this report word for word, because AI models are unpredictable, but it should come close.
